Like in the case of $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ , given a subset $S\subseteq W$ , define $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ to be the subcategory of $\mathscr{H}$ consisting of objects, all of whose perverse cohomologies are filtered colimits of extensions of $L_{w}$ for $w\in S$ , and define $\mathscr{H}^{S}$ to be the subcategory of $\mathscr{H}$ generated by $\pi_{!}P_{w}$ for $w\notin S$ .

#### Proposition 4.1.3.

The inclusion $\mathscr{H}^{S}\to\mathscr{H}$ admits a continuous right adjoint, $\mathscr{H}_{S}\to\mathscr{H}$ admits a continuous left adjoint, and

$$ \mathscr{H}^{S}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{S} $$

is a semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathscr{H}$ . Additionally, $\pi^{!}:\mathscr{H}\to\mathscr{O}_{0}$ sends $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ to $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ and $\mathscr{H}^{S}$ to $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ .

#### Proof.

As before, the inclusion $\mathscr{H}^{S}\to\mathscr{H}$ admits a continuous right adjoint because $\mathscr{H}^{S}$ is generated by objects which are compact in $\mathscr{H}$ . The assertion that $\mathscr{H}^{S,\perp}=\mathscr{H}_{S}$ follows from the fact that you can check whether $L_{w}$ appears as a composition factor of $x\in\mathscr{H}^{\heartsuit}$ after applying $\pi^{!}$ . This also shows that $\pi^{!}(\mathscr{H}_{S})\subseteq(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ .

It remains to show that $\pi^{!}(\mathscr{H}^{S})\subseteq(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ . We need to show that $\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w}\in(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ for $w\notin S$ . It suffices to show that

$$ \Hom(\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w},\mathscr{F})=0 $$

for all $\mathscr{F}\in(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ . Because $\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w}$ is compact, we can assume that $\mathscr{F}=L_{v}$ for $v\in S$ . By adjunction

$$ \Hom(\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w},L_{v})=\Hom(\pi^{*}\pi_{!}P_{w},L_{v})[-2\dim T]=\Hom(P_{w},\pi^{!}\pi_{*}L_{v})[-2\dim T]. $$

Since

$$ \pi^{!}\pi_{*}L_{v}\simeq C_{*}^{BM}(T)\otimes L_{v} $$

the result follows. ∎

#### 4.1.4.

Recall the notion of two-sided cells (already introduced in §1.2.3): if $\mathscr{H}_{w}^{\mathrm{access}}$ refers to the smallest two-sided ideal of $\mathscr{H}$ containing $L_{w}$ and stable under colimits and shifts, then we say that $v\leq_{LR}w$ if $L_{v}\in\mathscr{H}_{w}^{\mathrm{access}}$ . This defines a preorder on $W$ and the two-sided cells of $W$ are the corresponding partition: $w$ and $v$ lie in the same two-sided cell if $w\leq_{LR}v$ and $v\leq_{LR}w$ .

Let $c$ denote a two sided-cell in $W$ . Let $W_{\leq c}$ , $W_{<c}$ denote the subsets of $w\in W$ such that $w\leq_{LR}c$ and $w<_{LR}c$ , respectively. Denote the corresponding localizations of $\mathscr{H}$ by

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\text{ and }\mathscr{H}_{<c}, $$

respectively.

#### Proposition 4.1.4.

$\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ and $\mathscr{H}_{<c}$ are monoidal two-sided ideals in $\mathscr{H}$ .

#### Proof.

If $S$ is a subset of $W$ , then because $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under colimits and $\mathscr{H}$ is generated by $L_{w}$ for $w\in W$ , one can show that $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is a two-sided ideal in $\mathscr{H}$ just by showing that $L_{w}*(-)$ and $(-)*L_{w}$ preserve $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ . Every object $x\in\mathscr{H}_{S}$ can be written as the limit of its truncations for the t-structure

$$ x=\lim_{n}\tau_{\leq n}x, $$

and each $\tau_{\leq n}x$ can be written as a colimit of $L_{v}$ with $v\in S$ . Because $L_{w}$ is left- and right-dualizable and $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under limits as well as colimits, it suffices to show that $L_{w}*L_{v}$ and $L_{v}*L_{w}$ lie in $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ for all $v\in S$ . This is a direct consequence of the definition of two-sided cells (see §4.1.4). ∎

#### 4.1.5.

It follows from Proposition 4.1.3, Proposition 4.1.4, Proposition 2.1.0, and Proposition 2.1.0 that we obtain a system of semiorthogonal decompositions

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\not\leq c}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c} $$

where the subcategories of $\mathscr{H}$ admit monoidal structures making them semi-rigid monoidal categories, and the localization and colocalization functors are monoidal.

If we let $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ denote the left-orthogonal to $\mathscr{H}_{<c}$ inside of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ , then it follows from Proposition 2.1.0 and Proposition 2.1.0 that $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ admits a unique monoidal structure such that the projection $\mathscr{H}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is monoidal, and with respect to this monoidal structure $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ has the structure of a semi-rigid category. We also note that

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}\simeq\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\underset{\mathscr{H}}{\otimes}\mathscr{H}_{\not<c} $$

so we may think of the categories $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ as the associated-graded pieces of the system of semiorthogonal decompositions (18).

#### 4.1.6. Example

Let’s return to the case of $SL_{2}$ . Let $c$ denote the cell $\left\{1\right\}\subseteq W$ . Then $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is the subcategory of $\mathscr{H}$ generated by $\pi_{!}P_{1}$ .

$$ \pi_{i}\End(\pi_{!}P_{1})=\begin{cases}k&i=0,1\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

so it follows that $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ identifies with $\QCoh(\Omega\mathbf{A}^{1})$ as a plain dg category. One can show that the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ identifies with the monoidal structure on $\QCoh(\Omega\mathbf{A}^{1})$ coming from the group structure on $\Omega\mathbf{A}^{1}$ .

### 4.2. An action of the monoid $\mathbf{A}^{1}$

#### 4.2.1.

In [GLR26], we introduced a sheaf theory $\Sh(-)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ which is defined on schemes over $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ . If $X_{0}$ is a scheme over $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ whose base-change to $\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{q}$ is $X$ , then in keeping with the convention of loc. cit. we somewhat abusively denote the value of $\Sh(-)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ on $X_{0}$ by $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ . The definition of $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is as follows: the given $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ structure on $X$ equips this scheme with a geometric Frobenius endomorphism $\mathrm{Frob}$ , and

$$ \Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}\subseteq\Sh(X) $$

is the subcategory generated under colimits and shifts by irreducible perverse sheaves $\mathscr{F}\in\mathrm{Perv}(X)$ such that for some $n\geq 1$ there exists an isomorphism $\mathscr{F}\simeq(\mathrm{Frob}^{n})^{*}\mathscr{F}$ .

The important feature of $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is that it admits an action of a pro-algebraic group which we will denote $\mathbf{W}$ .55 5 This is the group which is denoted $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{alg,wt}}$ in loc. cit. This action is constructed using the theory of weights for $\ell$ -adic sheaves on varieties over finite fields and it has the property that $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{W}}$ is the category $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ (introduced in loc. cit.) which is a minor variant of the category of mixed sheaves (sometimes we will call an object of $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ a strongly mixed sheaf). If $\mathrm{Weil}_{q}\subseteq\overline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\times}$ denotes the subgroup of $q$ -Weil numbers, then $\mathbf{W}$ is the Cartier dual of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}$ . The homomorphism

$$ \mathrm{wt}:{\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}\to\mathbf{Z} $$

which sends a connected component of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}$ to the weight of its underlying Weil number gives rise to a distinguished subgroup ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}\subseteq\mathbf{W}$ after applying Cartier duality. The inclusion

$$ {\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}\subseteq{\mathbf{G}_{m}} $$

gives rise to a homomorphism $\mathrm{Frob}:\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{W}$ whose image is Zariski dense. One of the defining features of the action of $\mathbf{W}$ on $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is that the element $\mathrm{Frob}\in\mathbf{W}$ acts by pullback along geometric Frobenius.

#### 4.2.2.

Another feature of the action of $\mathbf{W}$ on $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is that the action of the weight ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ extends to an action of the commutative monoid scheme $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . In terms of Proposition 3.0.1 the category $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is a minor variant of the category of graded mixed sheaves introduced in [HL25], and the subcategory $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ is the category generated under colimits and shifts by perverse sheaves which are weight $\leq 0$ in the sense of [BBD82] (this category was considered previously in [Mor08]).

#### 4.2.3. Warning

The category $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ is not the derived category of mixed sheaves of weight $\leq 0$ in the sense of [BBD82]. Unlike the category defined in loc. cit., the category $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ is stable under shifts. This is advantageous for certain purposes, but it has the following drawback: if $f$ is a smooth proper map, then $f_{*}$ does not preserve weights in our sense.

#### 4.2.4.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a smooth morphism between schemes. Define the perverse pullback functor

$$ f^{!*}:\Sh(Y)^{\mathrm{relev}}\to\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}} $$

by

$$ f^{!*}=f^{*}[\dim(X/Y)]=f^{!}[-\dim(X/Y)]. $$

By construction, this functor is t-exact for the perverse t-structure. If we choose a square-root of $q$ , we can equip $f^{1/2}$ with the structure of equivariance for $\mathbf{W}$ as follows: consider the functor (which we will also denote $f^{1/2}$ ) from $\Sh(Y)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ to $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ defined by

$$ f^{!*}=f^{*}(\tfrac{\dim(X/Y)}{2})[\dim(X/Y)]=f^{!}(-\tfrac{\dim(X/Y)}{2})[-\dim(X/Y)]. $$

Then the functor between the categories of relevant sheaves arises as the de-equivariantization of this functor between the categories of strongly mixed sheaves, equipping it with equivariance data for $\mathbf{W}$ . It is easy to see that the functor $f^{!*}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant for the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action of §4.2.2.

If $\mathscr{Y}$ is an Artin stack, then define

$$ \Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}=\lim_{Y\to\mathscr{Y}}\Sh(Y)^{\mathrm{relev}} $$

where the limit is taken over all schemes $Y$ mapping smoothly to $\mathscr{Y}$ and the transition maps are the perverse pullback functors. In other words, $\Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is the full subcategory of $\Sh(\mathscr{Y})$ consisting of sheaves whose pullback to some (equiv. any) smooth cover is relevant. Taking the limit (19) internally to categories acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ defines a natural $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}$ . This $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action has the property that if $f:Y\to\mathscr{Y}$ is a smooth cover, then an object $\mathscr{F}$ of $\mathscr{Y}$ is in $\mathrm{Shv}(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ if and only if its pullback to $Y$ is, and similarly for $\mathrm{Shv}(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\geq 0}$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.4.

If $\mathscr{Y}=N\backslash G/B$ or $\mathscr{Y}=B\backslash G/B$ , then

$$ \Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}=\Sh(\mathscr{Y}). $$

#### Proof.

These categories are generated by the IC sheaves $L_{w}$ , whose pullbacks to $G/B$ are relevant. ∎

#### 4.2.5.

The above discussion shows that $\mathscr{H}$ acquires an action of the monoid $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . Since the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}\subseteq\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is compatible with six functors, the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}$ is compatible with this ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ action. However, we caution that because of the behavior described in §4.2.3, the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{H}$ is not compatible with its monoidal structure.

#### Proposition 4.2.5.

For any $S\subseteq W$ , the category $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{H}$ .

#### Proof.

The is follows by the arguments of [GLR26, §3.1]. In a little more detail, to show that $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , then as in the proof of [GLR26, Lemma 3.1.4] it suffices to show that the comonad

$$ \mathscr{H}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Av}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}\mathscr{H}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{oblv}}\mathscr{H} $$

preserves $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ . The comonad is t-exact (this can be checked after applying $\mathrm{oblv}$ to $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ , where it follows from the corresponding statement for schemes, which is the content of [GLR26, §2.6]), so it’s enough to check on objects in the heart. Since the comonad commutes with colimits, it suffices to show that it sends $L_{w}$ to an object of $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ for all $w\in S$ . Now each $L_{w}$ admits the structure of a strongly mixed sheaf, so the value of the comonad on $L_{w}$ is simply $\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\otimes L_{w}\in\mathscr{H}_{S}$ .

Once we know that $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , as in [GLR26, Proposition 3.1.7] to prove that it is stable under $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ it suffices to show that $\mathscr{H}_{S}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is preserved by the weight truncation functors on $\mathscr{H}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . The weight truncation functors are t-exact (again this follows by applying $\mathrm{oblv}$ to $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ ), so it suffices to check this for objects of the heart. Now the result follows because

$$ \tau_{\leq i}L_{w}=\begin{cases}L_{w}&i\geq 0\\
0&i<0\end{cases} $$

∎

By Proposition 4.2.5 the inclusions

$$ \mathscr{H}_{<c}\to\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H} $$

are $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. The left adjoints of these inclusions are left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, but we caution that the left adjoints are not strictly $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. By the compatibility of the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on $\mathscr{H}$ with smooth pullbacks (see §4.2.4) and Proposition 4.1.3 we see that the forgetful functor $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. By writing

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}\simeq\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}/\mathscr{H}_{<c} $$

$\mathscr{H}_{c}$ acquires an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ such that the projection $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is tautologically $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. We caution that the inclusion $\mathscr{H}_{c}\to\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is only left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant.

#### 4.2.6. Example

If we set $G=SL_{2}$ and take $c=\left\{1\right\}$ , then like in §4.1.2, one can calculate that

$$ H_{i}(\tau_{<c}(L_{1}))\simeq\begin{cases}L_{s}\left\langle-2i+1\right\rangle&i\geq 1\\
0&i<1\end{cases} $$

and

$$ H_{i}(\tau_{c}(L_{1}))\simeq\begin{cases}L_{s}\left\langle-2i-1\right\rangle&i>0\\
\nabla_{s}\left\langle-1\right\rangle&i=0\\
0&i<0\end{cases} $$

We note that for the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ defined above, the object $\tau_{c}(L_{1})$ is pure of weight zero (since it is the image of a sheaf which is pure of weight zero under $\tau_{c}$ ). However, the image of $\tau_{c}(L_{1})$ in $\mathscr{H}$ is evidently not pure of weight zero.

#### 4.2.7. Warning

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . By Proposition 3.0.1, the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{C}$ is completely determined by the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ plus the data of a certain full subcategory $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\subseteq\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . However, it is important to note that it may be the case that $\mathscr{C}$ has more automorphisms as a category acted on by ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ than it does as a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . This leads to a somewhat counterintuitive situation, where different choices of $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ can give rise to equivalent $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ actions on $\mathscr{C}$ . When this happens, the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -actions are equivalent via an isomorphism that induces a non-trivial automorphism of $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , which interchanges the two choices of $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ .

#### 4.2.8.

If $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category with an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , such that the monoidal structure is endowed with ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -equivariance data, we will say that the monoidal structure of $\mathscr{A}$ is left-compatible with the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{A}$ if the maps

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A} \displaystyle\mathrm{unit}:\Vect\to\mathscr{A} $$

have the property that the associated maps

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{mult}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}:\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\to\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}} \displaystyle\mathrm{unit}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}:\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}\to\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}} $$

factor through $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ .

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category equipped with an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , such that the monoidal structure is endowed with ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -equivariance data. Using Proposition 3.0.1, for any integer $k$ we can define a new category $\mathscr{A}(k)$ with an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , with ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -equivariant monoidal structure. Namely, $\mathscr{A}(k)=\mathscr{A}$ as a monoidal category acted on by ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , but $\mathscr{A}(k)^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}=\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n-k}$ . If we forget the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{A}$ , then $\mathscr{A}(k)$ and $\mathscr{A}$ are equivalent as plain categories acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ (acting by $\mathscr{O}(k)$ is a $\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ -linear automorphism of $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ that intertwines the two $\leq 0$ categories, as in §4.2.7). However, $\mathscr{A}(k)$ will not typically be equivalent to $\mathscr{A}$ as a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ with a ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -equivariant monoidal structure; in fact, it may be the case that the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{A}(k)$ is left-compatible with the monoidal structure, even when the action on $\mathscr{A}$ is not.

#### 4.2.9.

The monoidal structure of $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is not left-compatible with the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ as-is. However, let $a$ denote the value of Lusztig’s $a$ -function when evaluated on our given two-sided cell $c$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.9.

The monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}_{c}(a)$ is left-compatible with the natural action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ .

#### Proof.

Let’s first show that the unit of $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is concentrated in weights $\leq-a$ . Because the projection $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant and monoidal, it suffices to check that the unit of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is concentrated in weights $\leq-a$ . By the definition of the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ (see §4.2.5), we can check this after forgetting to $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ . We have an exact triangle

$$ \tau_{\leq-a}1_{\leq c}\to 1_{\leq c}\to\tau_{>-a}1_{\leq c} $$

coming from the semiorthogonal decomposition of $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}$ according to weights. It follows formally from the theory of semiorthogonal decompositions that the first map in this triangle is an isomorphism if and only if the second map is zero. Since

$$ \Hom_{(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq c}}(1_{\leq c},\tau_{>-a}1_{\leq c})\simeq\Hom_{(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}(1,\tau_{>-a}1_{\leq c}) $$

it suffices to show that the latter mapping space is zero. If we let $i$ denote the closed embedding $*/N\to N\backslash G/B$ , then this mapping space identifies with

$$ \Hom_{\Sh(*/N)^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}(\mathrm{triv},i^{!}\tau_{>-a}1_{\leq c}). $$

However, we claim that for any object $x$ of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ with weights strictly larger than $-a$ , the !-fiber $i^{!}x$ has weights strictly larger than zero (this immediately implies the vanishing of (20)). Since any such $x$ can be written as a limit of colimits of copies of $L_{w}\left\langle j\right\rangle$ , with $w\leq c$ and $j>-a$ , we can reduce to the case of $L_{w}\left\langle j\right\rangle$ . Now let $P_{w,v}$ denote the Kazhdan Lusztig polynomials. Define $p_{w,n}$ to be the coefficients of $P_{1,w}$ :

$$ P_{1,w}(q)=\sum p_{w,n}q^{n}. $$

By Kazhdan-Lusztig theory, we know that $i^{!}L_{w}$ is isomorphic to

$$ \bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\mathrm{triv}^{\oplus p_{w,n}}[2n-\ell(w)](n-\ell(w)/2). $$

If we let $\delta(w)$ denote the degree of $P_{1,w}$ , then by [Lus87, Equation 1.3.(a)] and [Lus85, Theorem 5.4] (see also [Cur88, Theorem 6.8.(i)] and [Cur88, Lemma 6.9.(ii)]) we know that for any $w\leq c$ ,

$$ 2\delta(w)-\ell(w)\leq-a(w). $$

It follows that $i^{!}L_{w}\left\langle j\right\rangle$ lies in weights strictly greater than zero in $\Sh(*/N)^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ for any $w\leq c$ and any $j>-a$ , as desired.

We now show that the product of two objects of $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ concentrated in weights $\leq-a$ remains in weights $\leq-a$ . Since the inclusion $\mathscr{H}_{c}\to\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ equivariant, if $x$ and $y$ are in weights $\leq-a$ as objects of $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , then they will be in weights $\leq-a$ as objects of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , as well. Since the projection $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, it suffices to show that for any $x,y\in\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ with weights $\leq 0$ , the truncation $\tau_{>a}(x*y)$ lies in $\mathscr{H}_{<c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . We will do this in 5 steps.

Step 1. Suppose that $x=L_{w}$ and $y=L_{v}$ for some $w,v\leq c$ . If either $x$ or $y$ is $<c$ , then $x*y$ is $<c$ . If both $x$ and $y$ lie in $c$ , then by purity $\tau_{>a}(x*y)$ lies in cohomological degree $>a$ . Now the result follows from [Lus97, §2.3].

Step 2. If both $x$ and $y$ are constructible, then the result follows from Step 1 because the condition that $\tau_{>a}(x*y)$ lies in $\mathscr{H}_{<c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is stable under the formation of finite colimits.

Step 3. Now suppose that $x$ is constructible and $y$ is compact. To show that $\tau_{>a}(x*y)$ lies in $\mathscr{H}_{<c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , it’s enough to check that all of its perverse cohomologies lie in $\mathscr{H}_{<c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . By [GLR26, Proposition 2.9.2], $\tau_{>a}$ is t-exact. Additionally, $x*(-)$ has finite cohomological amplitude, and because $x$ is dualizable it commutes with limits. Since every bounded below truncation $\tau^{p}_{\leq n}y$ of $y$ for the perverse t-structure is constructible, the result follows from Step 2.

Step 4. Suppose that both $x$ and $y$ are compact. Then $(-)*y$ has finite cohomological amplitude and because $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is semi-rigid, $y$ is dualizable. Then arguing like in Step 3 with the roles of $x$ and $y$ reversed, we may replace $x$ by its eventually coconnective truncations, which reduces to Step 3.

Step 5. If $x$ and $y$ are general objects of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ , then the result follows from Step 4 using the compact generation of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ and the compatibility of the monoidal structure with colimits. ∎

### 4.3. The asymptotic category

#### Construction 4.3.0.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category with an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ and suppose that the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{A}$ is left-compatible with the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . Then the category $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ acquires a natural $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action.

#### Proof.

The subcategory $\mathscr{A}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}_{\leq 0}$ is evidently a monoidal subcategory of $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . In the semiorthogonal decomposition

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq-1}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}} $$

the subcategory $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq-1}$ is a two-sided ideal inside of $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ , so like in the proof of Proposition 2.1.0, [Lur17, Proposition 2.2.1.9] equips $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ with a unique monoidal structure such that the projection $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\to\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is monoidal. ∎

#### 4.3.1.

Define $\mathscr{J}_{c}=\mathscr{H}_{c}(a)^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ . By Construction 4.3.0 this category acquires a natural monoidal structure. The goal of this section is to show that $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is equivalent as a monoidal category to Lusztig’s asymptotic category as defined in [Lus97, §2] (see also [EW21, §5]).

#### Proposition 4.3.1.

$\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is semisimple, and its simple objects are indexed by $w\in W_{\leq c}$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 4.1.3, $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is monadic over $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ . The monad is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant (it suffices to check this after including $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ into $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ ), so Proposition 3.4.1 shows that $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ admits a unique $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action such that the forgetful functor to $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. Since $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is monadic over $\mathscr{O}$ , and both the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action from §4.2.5 and this new one have the property that $\mathrm{oblv}$ is strictly $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, it follows from the uniqueness statement of Proposition 3.4.1 that the “new” $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action agrees with the one from §4.2.5.

It follows from the characterization of the category of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -invariants in Proposition 3.4.1 that $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is monadic over $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ . In fact, because $C_{*}(T)^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}=k$ , we know that

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\simeq(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}. $$

Now the result follows from [GLR26, Proposition 2.7.5]. ∎

#### Proposition 4.3.1.

$\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is semisimple, and its simple objects are indexed by $w\in c$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose that $x\in\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ . Then $x$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant as an object of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}(a)$ (for the rest of this proposition we will consider the $a$ -shifted $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ ). Applying the projection onto $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ to the exact triangle

$$ \tau_{\leq-1}x\to x\to\gr_{0}(x) $$

we see that $\tau_{\leq-1}x$ lies in $\mathscr{H}_{<c}$ and that $\tau_{\not<c}\gr_{0}(x)=x$ (here $\tau_{\leq-1}$ and $\gr_{0}$ refer to the weight filtration). In particular, every $x\in\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ arises as $\tau_{\not<c}y$ for $y\in\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ . By Proposition 4.3.1, $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is semisimple, with simple objects $L_{w}$ for $w\in W_{\leq c}$ . Since $\tau_{\not<c}L_{w}=0$ when $w<c$ , it remains to show that

$$ \Hom(\tau_{\not<c}L_{w},\tau_{\not<c}L_{v})=k^{\delta_{wv}} $$

for $w,v\in c$ . To see this, note that

$$ \Hom_{\mathscr{H}_{c}}(\tau_{\not<c}L_{w},\tau_{\not<c}L_{v})\simeq\Hom_{\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}}(\tau_{\not<c}L_{w},L_{v})\simeq\Hom_{\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}}(\tau_{\geq 0}\tau_{\not<c}L_{w},L_{v}), $$

so it’s enough to show that $\tau_{\geq 0}\tau_{\not<c}L_{w}\simeq L_{w}$ . Now note that there is a map

$$ \pi_{!}P_{w}\to L_{w} $$

in $\mathscr{H}$ which induces an isomorphism after applying $\tau_{\geq 0}$ (the weight truncation for $\mathscr{H}$ ). By the left-lax equivariance of the projector $\tau_{\leq c}$ , this implies that the map

$$ \tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}\to L_{w} $$

is also an isomorphism after applying $\tau_{\geq 0}$ . By the left-lax equivariance of $\tau_{\not<c}$ (viewed as an endofunctor of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ ), this implies that

$$ \tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}\simeq\tau_{\not<c}\tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}\to\tau_{\not<c}L_{w} $$

is an isomorphism after applying $\tau_{\geq 0}$ . Therefore

$$ \tau_{\geq 0}\tau_{\not<c}L_{w}\simeq\tau_{\geq 0}\tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}\simeq\tau_{\geq 0}L_{w}\simeq L_{w}, $$

as desired. ∎

#### 4.3.2.

In the context of the asymptotic category, we will write $J_{w}=\tau_{\not<c}L_{w}$ for the simple object corresponding to $w$ .

#### Proposition 4.3.2.

$\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is equivalent to Lustzig’s category as a monoidal category.

#### Proof.

By [Lur17, Corollary 5.4.4.7], it suffices to construct an equivalence of non-unital monoidal categories between our $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ and Lusztig’s category (indeed, every non-unital equivalence between unital monoidal categories is automatically quasi-unital). Unwinding the definition of the monoidal structure from Construction 4.3.0, we see that

$$ J_{w}*J_{v}=\tau_{\geq a}\tau_{\not<c}L_{w}*L_{v} $$

By purity, this agrees with

$$ H^{a}(\tau_{\not<c}L_{w}*L_{v}), $$

which is Lusztig’s definition of truncated convolution. ∎

#### 4.3.3.

Recall (see [Cur88, §6]) that an element $d$ in a cell $c$ is said to be a Duflo involution if

$$ a(d)=\ell(d)-2\delta(d) $$

(in [Lus87, §1] these elements are called “distinguished involutions”). This numerical equality implies, among other things, that $d$ has order 2 (see [Lus87, Proposition 1.4(a)], [Cur88, Theorem 6.8(iii)]).

#### Proposition 4.3.3.

The unit of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is

$$ \bigoplus_{d\in\mathscr{D}_{c}}J_{d}[-a] $$

where $\mathscr{D}_{c}$ is the set of Duflo involutions in the two-sided cell $c$ .

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from Proposition 4.3.1 and Lusztig’s description of the unit of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ (see [Lus97]). However, for completeness, we will give another proof of this, using the the fact that the unit of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ . Because the projection $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, we need to show that

$$ \tau_{\not<c}\tau_{\geq-a}1_{\leq c}\simeq\bigoplus_{d\in\mathscr{D}_{c}}L_{d}. $$

Arguing as in Proposition 4.2.9, we see that

$$ \tau_{\not<c}\tau_{\geq-a}1_{\leq c}\simeq\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in c\\
2\delta(w)-\ell(w)=-a\end{subarray}}L_{w}^{\oplus p_{w,\delta(w)}} $$

But Duflo involutions are definitionally elements of $c$ such that $\ell(w)-2\delta(w)=a$ , and it is well-known that for $d$ a Duflo involution, $p_{d,\delta(d)}=1$ (see [Lus87, Proposition 1.4(a)] or [Cur88, Theorem 6.8(iii)]). ∎

### 4.4. A variant: accessible sheaves

#### 4.4.1.

Let $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ generated under colimits and shifts by the irreducible objects $L_{w}$ with $w\leq c$ .

#### Proposition 4.4.1.

The category $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ is generated by objects which are compact in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ . (In fact, compact in $\mathscr{H}$ .)

#### Proof.

By Proposition 4.1.3, we may write

$$ L_{w}\simeq\colim_{\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}}(\pi_{!}\pi^{!})^{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}L_{w}, $$

where each term in the geometric realization lies in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ . Each term in the geometric realization is compact in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ by virtue of being compact in $\mathscr{H}$ , and each term is a finite extension of shifts of $L_{w}$ , so it lies in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ . ∎

#### 4.4.2.

It follows that we obtain a semiorthogonal decomposition

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}} $$

where $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}}$ is by definition the right orthogonal of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ .

#### 4.4.3. Example

Let’s consider the case when $G=SL_{2}$ and $c={s}\subseteq W$ . For simplicity, we will consider the category $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ , which is defined similarly to $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ . In this case, $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ identifies with the category denoted $\mathrm{QLisse}(\mathbf{P}^{1})$ in [AGK+22], which is the full subcategory of the unbounded derived category of sheaves consisting of objects whose perverse cohomology groups are (filtered colimits of) lisse sheaves. Infamously, this category is not the derived category of its heart. In fact something more is true, which is that this category is not even generated under colimits and shifts by objects in its heart (see loc. cit. §E.2.6).

The category $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ is the category denoted in loc. cit. by $\mathrm{IndLisse}(\mathbf{P}^{1})$ . It is exactly the full subcategory of $\mathrm{QLisse}(\mathbf{P}^{1})$ generated under colimits and shifts by objects in the heart. Here is an example of a sheaf $\mathscr{F}$ which lies in $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}}$ : consider an object such that

$$ H^{p}_{i}(\mathscr{F})=L_{s} $$

for all $i$ , and with the property that the map

$$ L_{s}[i]\to\tau_{\leq i}\mathscr{F}\xrightarrow{\partial}\tau_{>i}\mathscr{F}[1]\to L_{s}[i+2] $$

is a nonzero element in $H^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1})$ for all $i$ . Then

$$ \Hom(L_{s},\mathscr{F})=0 $$

so $\mathscr{F}$ lies in $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}}$ .

#### Proposition 4.4.3.

Suppose that $\mathscr{F}$ is a compact object of $\Sh(B\backslash G/B)$ and $\mathscr{G}$ is constructible. Then $\mathscr{F}*\mathscr{G}$ and $\mathscr{G}*\mathscr{F}$ are both compact.

#### Proof.

We may assume that $\mathscr{F}$ is of the form $\pi_{!}\mathscr{F}_{0}$ for some $\mathscr{F}_{0}\in\Sh(G/B)$ . By base change for the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G\times^{B}G/B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\backslash G\times^{B}G/B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/B\times B\backslash G/B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\backslash G/B\times B\backslash G/B} $$

it suffices to show that the pullback of $\mathscr{F}_{0}\boxtimes\mathscr{G}$ to $G\times^{B}G/B$ is compact. Because $G\times^{B}G/B$ is a scheme, its enough to check this after pulling back along the smooth cover $G\times^{B}G\to G\times^{B}G/B$ . Then the result follows because the pullback of $\mathscr{G}$ to $B\backslash G$ is compact. ∎

#### Proposition 4.4.3.

$\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ is a two-sided monoidal ideal in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to check that $x*y$ and $y*x$ lie in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ , where $x$ is a generator of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ and $y$ is a generator of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ . In particular, we may take $x=\tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}$ for $w\leq c$ and take $y=L_{v}$ for $v\leq c$ . Then we note that

$$ x*y=\pi_{!}P_{w}*L_{v} $$

is constructible, and similarly for $y*x$ . ∎

#### 4.4.4.

Now define

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}=\mathscr{H}_{c}\underset{\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}}{\otimes}\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}. $$

This is equivalently the full subcategory of $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ generated by $\tau_{c}(L_{w})$ for $w\in c$ .

## 5. A categorification of Lusztig’s homomorphism

#### 5.0.1.

Recall from §1.2.15 the Lusztig’s homomorphism

$$ \psi_{c}:H\to J_{c}[t^{\pm 1}] $$

such that

$$ \psi_{c}(b_{w})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in c\\
d\in\mathscr{D}_{c}\end{subarray}}h_{w,d,v}(t)j_{v}. $$

The fact that this map defines an algebra homomorphism is highly non-obvious, and in fact the following example shows that the map $\psi_{c}$ cannot be naively categorified to produce a monoidal functor from $\mathscr{H}$ to $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ .

Let $G$ be $SL_{3}$ and let $s$ and $t$ denote the simple reflections of the Weyl group. Take $c$ to be the two-sided cell $\left\{s,t,st,ts\right\}$ . Then

$$ \psi_{c}(b_{s})=j_{st}-(t+t^{-1})j_{s}. $$

However, the object $L_{s}\in\mathscr{H}$ is self-dual, while the object

$$ J_{st}\oplus J_{s}\left\langle-1\right\rangle[1]\oplus J_{s}\left\langle 1\right\rangle[-1]\in\mathscr{J}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}} $$

is not self-dual (because $J_{st}^{\vee}=J_{ts}$ ), so there cannot be a monoidal functor from $\mathscr{H}$ to $\mathscr{J}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ sending $L_{s}$ to $J_{st}\oplus J_{s}\left\langle-1\right\rangle[1]\oplus J_{s}\left\langle 1\right\rangle[-1]$ .

Nevertheless, in this section, we will show that after performing an additional categorification it is possible to construct an analogue of Lusztig’s homomorphism. Namely, we will show that there is a map

$$ \mathscr{H}\textrm{-mod}\to\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}. $$

In §6, we will apply trace of Frobenius to this map to recover the classification of unipotent representations.

The outline of this section is as follows:

- – In §5.1 we will construct a monoidal category $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ which is Morita-equivalent to $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ .

- – In §5.2 we show that the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is strictly compatible with the monoidal structure.

- – In §5.3 we prove some technical results showing that two a priori different monoidal structures on $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ are the same.

### 5.1. A monoidal category Morita equivalent to $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$

#### 5.1.1.

If $\mathscr{A}$ is a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ and $\mathscr{A}$ has a monoidal structure which is left-compatible with the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action, then we have a diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F} $$

where both arrows are monoidal by Construction 4.3.0. The inclusion of $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ into $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ identifies with

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\xrightarrow{F^{R}}\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\to\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}, $$

so it acquires a lax-monoidal structure. As a result, the unit of $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ , which is by definition $\gr_{0}(1)$ , acquires the structure of an algebra object in $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ .

#### 5.1.2.

Applying the paradigm of §5.1.1 to the case when $\mathscr{A}=\mathscr{H}_{c}$ , we obtain an algebra structure on $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ . The category $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}=\gr_{0}(1_{c})\mathrm{-bimod}(\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ is monadic over $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , and the monad preserves the subcategory $\mathscr{H}_{c,\leq 0}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . It follows from Proposition 3.4.1 that $\mathscr{B}_{c}=\gr_{0}(1_{c})\mathrm{-bimod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})$ admits a unique $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action such that

$$ \mathrm{oblv}:\mathscr{B}_{c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c} $$

is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. Similar considerations apply to the categories of left- and right-modules for $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ in $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ .

The remainder of the current subsection is devoted to proving that $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is Morita equivalent to $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ .

#### Proposition 5.1.2.

The category $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is semi-rigid.

#### Proof.

The functor

$$ \mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{B}_{c}\otimes\mathscr{B}_{c}\to\mathscr{B}_{c} $$

is obtained from

$$ (-)\underset{\gr_{0}(1_{c})}{*}(-):\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\otimes\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\to\mathscr{H}_{c} $$

by applying

$$ \gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}\underset{\mathscr{H}_{c}}{\otimes}(-)\underset{\mathscr{H}_{c}}{\otimes}\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c}), $$

so it suffices to show that (21) admits a continuous $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ -bilinear right adjoint.

$\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})$ is compactly generated by objects of the form $\gr_{0}(1_{c})*x$ , where $x$ is compact in $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ . Similarly, $\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})$ is compactly generated by objects of the form $y*\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ , so to show that (21) admits a continuous right adjoint it’s enough to show that

$$ y*\gr_{0}(1_{c})*x $$

is compact in $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ . Since $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is compactly generated by objects of the form $\tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}$ for $w\in W_{c}$ , it’s enough to show that

$$ \tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})*\tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{v} $$

is compact. Since $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ already lies in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ , this product identifies with

$$ \pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})*\pi_{!}P_{v}. $$

Now compactness follows from by Proposition 4.4.3, which says that the convolution of a constructible object with a compact object of $\mathscr{H}$ is again compact. Recall (see §4.1.5) that $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is semi-rigid, and (21) is evidently $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ -bilinear, so we know that the right adjoint of (21) is also $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ -bilinear. ∎

#### Proposition 5.1.2.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category and $x\in\mathrm{Alg}(\mathscr{A})$ is an algebra in $\mathscr{A}$ . Let $\mathscr{B}$ denote $x\textrm{-bimod}(\mathscr{A})$ . Then $x\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{A})$ is left-dualizable as a $(\mathscr{B},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodule, with left dual $x\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{A})$ .

#### Proof.

The unit of the duality is the natural isomorphism

$$ \epsilon:\mathscr{B}\simeq x\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{A})\underset{\mathscr{A}}{\otimes}x\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{A}). $$

The counit

$$ \eta:x\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{A})\underset{\mathscr{B}}{\otimes}x\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{A})\to\mathscr{A} $$

is the map coming from $(-)\underset{x}{*}(-)$ . The triangle identities follow by unwinding the definitions. ∎

#### Proposition 5.1.2.

The category $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is Morita equivalent to $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ .

#### Proof.

Proposition 5.1.2 shows that

$$ (\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c}),\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})) $$

is a pair of adjoint functors between $\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod}$ and $\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod}$ . Note that the counit map

$$ \eta:\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\underset{\mathscr{B}_{c}}{\otimes}\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\to\mathscr{H}_{c} $$

admits a continuous $(\mathscr{H}_{c},\mathscr{H}_{c})$ -bilinear right adjoint: indeed, bilinearity is automatic from the semi-rigidity of $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ , and because $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is rigid, it suffices to check that the map

$$ \gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\otimes\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\to\mathscr{H}_{c} $$

admits a continuous right adjoint. The category $\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})$ is compactly generated by objects of the form $x=x_{0}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ with $x_{0}$ compact in $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ , and similarly for $\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})$ . The map (22) sends

$$ x\otimes y\mapsto x\underset{\gr_{0}(1_{c})}{*}y, $$

and if $x=x_{0}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ and $y=\gr_{0}(1_{c})*y_{0}$ , the image is $x_{0}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})*y_{0}$ , which is compact in $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ by Proposition 4.4.3.

It follows by [BZGO20, Theorem 1.3] (see also [BLR24, Proposition 4.2.4]) that $\eta$ is fully faithful, so it remains to check that its essential image is $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ . Because $x_{0}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})*y_{0}$ lies in $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ , we know that

$$ \gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\underset{\mathscr{B}_{c}}{\otimes}\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}} $$

Conversely, given any $w\in c$ , the irreducible $L_{w}$ lies in the image of

$$ \mathrm{oblv}:\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\to\mathscr{H}_{c}, $$

so every sheaf in $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ lies in the image of $\eta$ . ∎

### 5.2. Analysis of the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action

#### 5.2.1.

The goal of this section is to analyze the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ , which was defined in §5.1.2.

#### Proposition 5.2.1.

$$ \mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\simeq\mathscr{J}_{c}. $$

#### Proof.

Proposition 3.4.1 shows that, $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is monadic over $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}=\mathscr{J}_{c}$ , and the monad identifies with the zeroth graded piece of

$$ \gr_{0}(1_{c})*(-)*\gr_{0}(1_{c}). $$

However, this is just the identity endofunctor of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ , so we see that the equivalence

$$ \mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\simeq\mathscr{J}_{c} $$

follows from the following (well-known) Lemma 5.2.1, applied to the monoidal category $\mathscr{C}=\End(\mathscr{J}_{c})$ . ∎

#### Lemma 5.2.1.

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a monoidal category. If $x\in\mathrm{Alg}(\mathscr{C})$ is an algebra object such that $x$ is isomorphic to the unit $1$ as a plain object of $\mathscr{C}$ , then the unit map $1\to x$ is an isomorphism in $\mathrm{Alg}(\mathscr{C})$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to show that the unit map $1\to x$ is an isomorphism in $\mathscr{C}$ . If we write $\alpha:x\simeq 1$ for the given isomorphism between $x$ and $1$ , then it suffices to show that

$$ x\xrightarrow{\alpha}1\xrightarrow{\mathrm{unit}}x $$

is an isomorphism. Because $\End(x)\simeq\End(1)$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -algebra, once we know that endomorphism has a left-inverse, it follows that it is invertible. Tensoring $\mathrm{unit}:1\to x$ with $\alpha:x\to 1$ , we obtain a commutative square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x\otimes x} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{unit}\otimes\id} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\otimes\alpha} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{unit}} $$

so the existence of the desired left-inverse follows from the fact that $\mathrm{mult}$ is a left inverse of $\mathrm{unit}\otimes\id$ . ∎

#### 5.2.2.

We now wish to show that the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is strictly compatible with the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ . First, we note that the argument of Proposition 5.2.1 also applies to the categories of left- and right-modules for $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ in $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ . This implies the following technical result which will be useful shortly:

#### Proposition 5.2.2.

Suppose that $x\in\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ is concentrated in a single graded degree. Then any summand of $x$ as a plain object of $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is naturally a summand of $x$ as a right $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ -module.

#### Proof.

Follows from the fact that $\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\simeq\mathscr{J}_{c}\simeq\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ , which is proved like in Proposition 5.2.1. ∎

#### 5.2.3.

For any $w\in c$ , the object $L_{w}$ is concentrated in a single graded degree, so it naturally acquires the structure of a $\gr_{0}(1)$ -bimodule. Our next result will be a technical statement about the convolution

$$ L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}. $$

Before we state it, let us recall some facts about left cells:

- (1) Every left cell contains a unique Duflo involution [Lus87, Theorem 1.10] (see also [Cur88, Theorem 6.11]).

- (2) If $w$ and $v$ lie in the same left cell, then there is a sequence of elements

$$ v=u_{0},u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}=w $$

with each $u_{i}$ lying in $c$ , such that for each $i$ between $1$ and $n$ there is a simple reflection $s_{i}$ such that $s_{i}u_{i-1}>u_{i-1}$ (for the Bruhat order), and $L_{u_{i}}$ appears as a direct summand of $L_{s_{i}}*L_{u_{i-1}}$ [Cur88, Lemma 5.3.(ii)] (of course this follows from the material of [KL79]).

#### Proposition 5.2.3.

For $w,v\in c$ , the weights of

$$ L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v} $$

are bounded from below. In other words, this object lies in $\mathscr{H}_{c,\geq N}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ for some $N$ .

#### Proof.

If $w$ is a Duflo involution, then it is a summand of $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ (necessarily as a right $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ -module by Proposition 5.2.2). It follows that

$$ L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v} $$

is a summand of

$$ \gr_{0}(1)\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\simeq L_{v} $$

so the result follows when $w$ is a Duflo involution. Now suppose that $w$ is an arbitrary element of $c$ . Let $d$ denote the unique Duflo involution lying in the left cell containing $w$ . We know that there is some sequence

$$ d=u_{0},u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}=w $$

as in §5.2.3(2). Arguing by induction on the minimal length of such a sequence, we may assume that there is some $x\in c$ and some simple reflection $s$ such that

$$ L_{x}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{w} $$

has weights bounded from below, $sx>x$ , and $L_{w}$ appears as a direct summand of $L_{s}*L_{x}$ . By the assumption that $sx>x$ , we know that $L_{s}*L_{x}$ is concentrated in a single graded degree, so $L_{w}$ is a summand of $L_{s}*L_{x}$ as a right $\gr_{0}(1)$ -module. It follows that

$$ L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v} $$

is a summand of

$$ (L_{s}*L_{x})\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\simeq L_{s}*\left(L_{x}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right), $$

so its weights are bounded from below. ∎

#### Lemma 5.2.3.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is monoidal compatibly with the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , and that the monoidal structure is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. If the unit of $\mathscr{A}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}$ lies in degree zero and the multiplication preserves $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{=0}$ , then the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on $\mathscr{A}$ is strictly compatible with the monoidal structure.

#### Proof.

The only thing that needs to be checked is that the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ preserves $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\geq 0}$ . But every object of $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\geq 0}$ can be written as a colimit of terms concentrated in a single degree, so the result follows from the compatibility of $\mathrm{mult}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ with colimits and the action of $\mathscr{O}(n)$ . ∎

#### Proposition 5.2.3.

The $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is strictly compatible with the monoidal structure.

#### Proof.

It is obvious that $\gr_{0}(1)$ lies in degree zero. By Lemma 5.2.3 it remains to show that for any irreducibles $L_{w}$ , $L_{v}$ the map

$$ L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\to\gr_{0}(L_{w}*L_{v}) $$

is an isomorphism. It’s enough to do this after forgetting the $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ -bimodule structure on both sides. The morphism $1_{c}\to\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ of algebras in $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ induces a map of simplicial objects

$$ \mathrm{Bar}(L_{w},1_{c},L_{v})\to\mathrm{Bar}(L_{w},\gr_{0}(1_{c}),L_{v}) $$

which becomes an isomorphism after applying $\tau_{\geq 0}$ . This shows that (23) becomes an isomorphism after applying $\tau_{\geq 0}$ , so it remains to show that

$$ \gr_{k}\left(L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)=0 $$

for all $k<0$ . Because there are only finitely many elements in $c$ , Proposition 5.2.3 shows that there is some $N$ such that

$$ \gr_{k}\left(L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)=0 $$

for all $w,v\in c$ and $k<N$ . Now it suffices to show that if $k<0$ , and

$$ \gr_{\ell}\left(L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)=0 $$

for all $\ell<k$ and all $w\in c$ , then

$$ \gr_{k}\left(L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)=0. $$

To see this, consider the object $L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1)$ , the free right $\gr_{0}(1)$ -module on $L_{w}$ . By Verdier duality we know that $L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1)$ lies in weight $\geq-2a$ and $\gr_{-2a}(L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1))\simeq L_{w}[2a]$ . Additionally,

$$ \left(L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1)\right)\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\simeq L_{w}*L_{v}, $$

so we obtain an exact triangle

$$ L_{w}[2a]\left\langle-2a\right\rangle\underset{\gr_{0}(1_{c})}{*}L_{v}\to L_{w}*L_{v}\to\tau_{>-2a}(L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1))\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}. $$

Since $L_{w}*L_{v}$ lies in degree $\geq-2a$ , for any $k<0$ we obtain an isomorphism

$$ \gr_{k-2a}\left(\tau_{>-2a}(L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1))\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)[-1]\simeq\gr_{k-2a}\left(L_{w}\left\langle-2a\right\rangle\underset{\gr_{0}(1_{c})}{*}L_{v}\right)[2a] $$

so in other words

$$ \gr_{k}\left(L_{w}\underset{\gr_{0}(1_{c})}{*}L_{v}\right)\simeq\gr_{k-2a}\left(\tau_{>-2a}(L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1))\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)[-1-2a]. $$

$\tau_{>-2a}(L_{w}*\gr_{0}(1))$ is an iterated extension of objects of the form

$$ L_{u}[i]\left\langle-i\right\rangle $$

for $i<2a$ . By our inductive assumption

$$ \gr_{k-2a}\left(L_{u}[i]\left\langle-i\right\rangle\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)[-1-2a]\simeq\gr_{k-2a+i}\left(L_{u}\underset{\gr_{0}(1)}{*}L_{v}\right)[i-1-2a]=0, $$

so the result follows. ∎

### 5.3. The monoidal structure of the category of invariants

#### 5.3.1.

If $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ (strictly), the category $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ acquires a monoidal structure by functoriality. On the other hand, because the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action is left-compatible with the monoidal structure (in the sense of §4.2.8), Construction 4.3.0 equips $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ with an a priori different monoidal structure. The goal of this subsection is to show that these two monoidal structures agree.

#### Proposition 5.3.1.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category, equipped with a semiorthogonal decomposition

$$ \mathscr{A}_{\ell}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}_{r} $$

such that $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ is a (unital) monoidal subcategory of $\mathscr{A}$ and $\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ is a two-sided ideal. Then the two monoidal structures on $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ (as a subcategory and as a quotient of $\mathscr{A}$ ) agree.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathscr{A}_{r}^{\mathrm{sub}}$ denote $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ , viewed as having the subcategory monoidal structure, and let $\mathscr{A}_{r}^{\mathrm{quot}}$ denote $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ with the quotient monoidal structure. If we write $i:\mathscr{A}_{r}\to\mathscr{A}$ for the inclusion, then the composite

$$ \mathscr{A}_{r}^{\mathrm{sub}}\xrightarrow{i}\mathscr{A}\xrightarrow{i^{L}}\mathscr{A}_{r}^{\mathrm{quot}} $$

is a monoidal equivalence between $\mathscr{A}_{r}^{\mathrm{sub}}$ and $\mathscr{A}_{r}^{\mathrm{quot}}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 5.3.1.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ (strictly). Then the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ of Construction 4.3.0 realizes $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ as the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -invariants of the monoidal category $\mathscr{A}$ .

#### Proof.

Regarding $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ as the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -invariants of the monoidal category $\mathscr{A}$ , there is a canonical monoidal functor $i:\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\to\mathscr{A}$ . Equivariantizing, we obtain a monoidal functor

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})\simeq(\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\xrightarrow{i^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}} $$

(the first equivalence holds because the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ (and hence ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ ) on $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is canonically trivial). The composite

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{wt}_{0}}\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{oblv}}\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}} $$

is a monoidal equivalence (as it is a composite of monoidal functors, and it is an equivalence). Moreover, the functor

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{wt}_{0}}\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})\xrightarrow{i^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}} $$

is fully faithful, so we see that the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ coming from the fact that it is the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -invariants of $\mathscr{A}$ identifies with the monoidal structure it acquires as a subcategory of $\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . Now the result follows by applying Proposition 5.3.1 to

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq-1}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}. $$

∎

#### Corollary 5.3.1.

The functor $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}:\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ acquires a natural monoidal structure making the following diagrams commute

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{oblv}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{act}_{0})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}}}}} $$

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{oblv}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}}}}} $$

(as diagrams of monoidal functors).

#### Proof.

By Proposition 3.1.1, there is a monoidal functor $r:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ , making the diagrams

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{act}_{0}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} $$

commute (as $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant monoidal categories). Forgetting the monoidal structure, we obtain similar diagrams of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant categories. However, the de-equivariantizations of (24, 25) are diagrams of the same shape, so we obtain natural isomorphisms $r\simeq(\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}})^{\mathrm{deeq}}$ and $i\simeq\mathrm{oblv}^{\mathrm{deeq}}$ of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant functors. This gives the desired upgrade of $(\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}})^{\mathrm{deeq}}$ to an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant monoidal functor. ∎

#### 5.3.2.

We will end by using the monoidal structure on $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}$ to give a new proof of the rigidity of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ . This was first proved for affine and finite Weyl groups in [BFO09, §4.3] by explicitly describing $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ (see [EW21, §5] for more discussion and a proof for more general Coxeter groups). This result will be used later in §6.

#### Proposition 5.3.2.

The functor $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}$ admits a continuous right adjoint and the category $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is rigid.

#### Proof.

$\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is compactly generated by (shifts and Tate twists of) objects of the form

$$ \gr_{0}(1_{c})*\tau_{\leq c}\pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})\simeq\gr_{0}(1_{c})*\pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c}) $$

for $w\in c$ (here we have used the fact that $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ , being a direct sum of irreducibles in $c$ , already lies in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ ). By Proposition 4.4.3, the object $\gr_{0}(1_{c})*\pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ is compact in $\mathscr{H}$ , so it lies in finitely many graded degrees and its associated graded pieces are direct sums of finitely many irreducible objects. It follows that $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}(\gr_{0}(1_{c})*\pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c}))$ is compact in $\mathscr{J}_{c}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ . This shows that $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}$ admits a continuous right adjoint.

To see that $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is rigid, first note that the unit $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ is compact so it suffices to show that every compact object is left- and right-dualizable. Since $\mathrm{oblv}:\mathscr{J}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is monoidal, it suffices to show that $J_{w}$ , viewed as an object of $\mathscr{J}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ living in weight zero, is left- and right-dualizable. However, $J_{w}$ is a summand of $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}(\gr_{0}(1_{c})*\pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c}))$ (being the zeroth graded peice). Since $\gr_{0}(1_{c})*\pi_{!}P_{w}*\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ is compact, it is left- and right-dualizable (as $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is semi-rigid). By Corollary 5.3.1, applied with $\mathscr{A}=\mathscr{B}_{c}$ , we know that $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}$ is monoidal, which shows that $J_{w}$ is a summand of a left- and right-dualizable object. ∎

## 6. Unipotent representations

#### 6.0.1.

The goal of this section is to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.4.

The outline of this section is as follows:

- – In §6.1 we show that the prior work of Soergel and Wendt on mixed Tate motives implies that the action of Frobenius on $\mathscr{H}$ identifies with the action of $\sqrt{q}$ , with respect to the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action of §4.2.

- – In §6.2 we show that $HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})$ agrees with $HH(\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}};\mathrm{Frob})$ using the equivalence $HH(\mathscr{H};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}$ .

- – In §6.3 we show that every action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ on a semisimple category is trivial and give a criterion for an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action to be trivial.

- – In §6.4 we employ a certain renormalization of $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ to show that the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $HH(\mathscr{B}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})$ is trivial.

- – In §6.5 we finish the proof of Theorem 1.1.4.

### 6.1. Motives and the action of $\mathbf{W}$

#### 6.1.1.

Recall the group $\mathbf{W}$ from §4.2.1. Let $\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}$ denote the monoidal category which is equal to $\mathscr{H}$ as a plain category, but whose monoidal structure is given by !-pull (as opposed to perverse pullback) and *-push along the correspondence

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\backslash G\times^{B}G/B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\backslash G/B\times B\backslash G/B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\backslash G/B} $$

As in §4.2, $\mathbf{W}$ acts on $\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}$ compatibly with its monoidal structure.

Now let $\pi:\mathbf{W}\to{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ denote the map which is Cartier dual to the map $\mathbf{Z}\to\mathrm{Weil}_{q}$ sending 1 to $q$ .

#### Proposition 6.1.1.

The action of $\mathbf{W}$ on $\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}$ factors through $\pi:\mathbf{W}\to{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ compatibly with the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to show an equivalence of $\Rep(\mathbf{W})$ -linear monoidal categories

$$ \mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive},\mathbf{W}}\simeq\Rep(\mathbf{W})\underset{\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})}{\otimes}\mathscr{C} $$

for some monoidal category $\mathscr{C}$ acted on by $\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ . As in [SW18], let $\mathscr{C}$ denote the category of $\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}$ -linear stratified mixed Tate motives on $B\backslash G/B$ . This category is monoidal by the compatibility of stratified mixed Tate motives with pushforward along Whitney-Tate maps (see [RS20, §3.1]). There is a natural $\ell$ -adic realization functor $\mathscr{C}\to\mathrm{Shv}(B\backslash G/B)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ which is compatible with six functors. In particular, it is monoidal and linear for the action of $DTM(\Spec\mathbf{F}_{q})$ . By the vanishing of the rational higher $K$ -theory of $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ , we know that $DTM(\Spec\mathbf{F}_{q})\simeq\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ . We therefore obtain a map of $\Rep(\mathbf{W})$ -linear monoidal categories

$$ \Rep(\mathbf{W})\underset{\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})}{\otimes}\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive},\mathbf{W}}. $$

It suffices to show that this map is an equivalence after de-equivariantiztion for $\mathbf{W}$ , where the result follows from [SW18, Theorem 3(2)]. ∎

#### 6.1.2. Remark

The appearance of motives in the above proof is not really necessary for our present purposes; we will briefly sketch an alternative approach just involving $\ell$ -adic sheaves. One could take $\mathscr{C}$ to be the category of stratified Tate $\ell$ -adic sheaves in the sense of [AR13, §7.2] (the category which is called $D^{\mathrm{mix}}_{\mathscr{S}}(X)$ in loc. cit.). Perhaps up to some difficulties with homotopy coherence, the “genuineness” results of [AR13, §9] imply that this category is monoidal (and one can imagine getting around the homotopy coherence problem using the t-structure on $D^{\mathrm{mix}}_{\mathscr{S}}(X)$ ). Then [AR13, Proposition 7.5(ii)] implies that the natural functor $\Rep(\mathbf{W})\underset{\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})}{\otimes}\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive},\mathbf{W}}$ is an isomorphism.

#### 6.1.3.

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a monoidal category and $x\in\mathrm{Alg}(\mathscr{C})$ . We will say that a map

$$ \ell:1\to x $$

is an invertible point of $x$ if the composition

$$ x\xrightarrow{\id\otimes\ell}x\otimes x\xrightarrow{\mathrm{mult}}x $$

is an isomorphism. Given such an $\ell$ , the object $x$ acquires a new algebra structure by transport of structure along the isomorphism (26). Concretely, if $\mathscr{C}=\mathrm{dgCat}$ , $x=\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal category, and $\ell=\mathscr{L}$ is an invertible object of $\mathscr{A}$ , then the new monoidal structure on $\mathscr{A}$ has multiplication map

$$ x*^{\mathscr{L}}y\simeq x*\mathscr{L}*y $$

and unit $\mathscr{L}^{{}^{-1}}$ . Note that the modified multiplication is indeed associative, because

$$ (x*\mathscr{L}*y)*\mathscr{L}*z\simeq x*\mathscr{L}*(y*\mathscr{L}*z). $$

#### 6.1.4.

If we pick a choice $v$ of a square-root of $q$ , we obtain a retract $r$ of the map ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathbf{W}$ . The kernel of the retract lies in the kernel of $\pi$ , and the following diagram commutes

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{W}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(-)^{2}} $$

For clarity of notation, going forward we will denote this new copy of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ which is the image of $r$ by ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{1/2}$ .

#### Proposition 6.1.4.

The action of $\mathbf{W}$ on $\mathscr{H}$ factors through $r:\mathbf{W}\to{\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{1/2}$ compatibly with the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}$ .

#### Proof.

Since the action of $\mathbf{W}$ on $\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}$ factors through ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , it factors through ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{1/2}$ as well. Now apply the construction of §6.1.3 where $\mathscr{C}={\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{1/2}\textrm{-Cat}$ and $x=\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}$ , and $\ell$ is the object

$$ \mathscr{O}(\dim B)[-\dim B]\otimes 1_{\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}} $$

of

$$ \Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{1/2})\underset{\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})}{\otimes}\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}\simeq\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive},{\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{1/2}}\simeq\Hom_{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{1/2}}(\Vect,\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{naive}}). $$

∎

### 6.2. Calculating the trace of $\mathscr{H}^{\mathrm{inaccess}}$

#### 6.2.1.

The arguments of [Ete25, §6.3] show that

$$ \tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}\textrm{-mod})\simeq\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}} $$

in such a way that the canonical trace map

$$ \mathscr{H}\to\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}\textrm{-mod}) $$

identifies with pull-push along the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/\mathrm{Ad}_{\mathrm{Frob}}(B)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\backslash G/B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/\mathrm{Ad}_{\mathrm{Frob}}(G)} $$

However, this result is not stated as-is in loc. cit, so for the sake of completeness we note that this follows directly from [Zhu25, Proposition 8.57]. Namely, in the notation of loc. cit, let $X=BB$ , let $Y=BG$ , and let $f:X\to Y$ denote the natural map. Let $\phi_{X}$ and $\phi_{Y}$ denote the respective Frobenius endomorphisms. Let $Z=Y$ , let $g_{1}=\id$ , and let $g_{2}=\phi_{Y}$ . Since $f$ is proper and $\Delta_{X}$ is smooth, the assumptions of the proposition are satisfied. Therefore we learn that the category

$$ HH(\mathscr{H};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\Sh(X\times_{Y}X);\mathrm{Frob}) $$

identifies with the full subcategory of

$$ \Sh(Y\times_{Y\times Y}Z)\simeq\Sh(G/\mathrm{Ad}_{\mathrm{Frob}}(G))\simeq\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q})) $$

generated by pull-push along

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times_{Y\times Y}Z} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times X\times_{Y\times Y}Z} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y\times_{Y\times Y}Z} $$

in such a way that the canonical trace functor identifies with pull-push along this diagram. However, after unwinding definitions this push-pull diagram identifies with (27). The functor of pull-push along (27) is precisely Deligne-Lusztig induction with trivial central character, so indeed

$$ HH(\mathscr{H};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}} $$

(essentially by the definition [DL76, Definition 7.8] of what it means for a representation to be unipotent).

#### Proposition 6.2.1.

$$ \tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}}\textrm{-mod})=0. $$

#### Proof.

Applying Construction 2.2.2 to the semiorthogonal decomposition

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}} $$

we see that it’s enough to show that the composite

$$ \tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\textrm{-mod})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{oblv}}\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}} $$

is conservative, where the second arrow is the natural projection from (28). Because $\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\textrm{-mod})$ is semisimple, it’s enough to show that the image of any simple object under $\mathrm{oblv}$ is constructible. We can check this after including $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ into $\mathscr{H}$ , and applying Construction 2.2.2 to the semiorthogonal decomposition

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\not\leq c}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c} $$

we see that

$$ \tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\textrm{-mod})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{oblv}}\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H} $$

identifies with

$$ \tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\textrm{-mod})\to\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}\textrm{-mod})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{oblv}}\mathscr{H}. $$

§6.2.1 shows that $\mathrm{oblv}$ identifies with pull-push along the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/\mathrm{Ad}_{\mathrm{Fr}}(B)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G/\mathrm{Ad}_{\mathrm{Fr}}(G)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\backslash G/B} $$

and because $G/\mathrm{Ad}_{\mathrm{Fr}}(B)\to B\backslash G/B$ is schematic, *-push preserves constructibility. ∎

#### Proposition 6.2.1.

$$ HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{B}_{c};\mathrm{Frob}) $$

#### Proof.

Since

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}}=\mathscr{H}_{c}\underset{\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}}{\otimes}\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}} $$

is a coreflective subcategory of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}}$ , it follows from Construction 2.2.2 and Proposition 6.2.1 that

$$ HH(\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{inaccess}};\mathrm{Frob})=0. $$

Applying Construction 2.2.2 again we see that

$$ HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}};\mathrm{Frob}). $$

Now the result follows from Proposition 5.1.2 ∎

### 6.3. Actions on semisimple categories

#### Proposition 6.3.0.

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a split semisimple dg category. Every action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ on $\mathscr{C}$ is (noncanonically) trivializable.

#### Proof.

Let’s write $\mathscr{C}\simeq\Vect^{I}$ and let $\mathrm{ins}_{i}:\Vect\to\mathscr{C}$ and $\ev_{i}:\mathscr{C}\to\Vect$ denote insertion and evaluation functors corresponding to $i\in I$ . Let $\mathscr{F}^{i}_{j}\in\QCoh({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ denote

$$ \ev_{j}\circ\ \mathrm{coact}\circ\mathrm{ins}_{i}(k). $$

The definition of a coaction implies that

$$ \displaystyle i_{1}^{*}(\mathscr{F}^{i}_{j}) \displaystyle\simeq k^{\delta_{ij}} \displaystyle\mathrm{mult}^{*}(\mathscr{F}^{i}_{j}) \displaystyle\simeq\bigoplus_{k}\mathscr{F}^{i}_{k}\boxtimes\mathscr{F}^{k}_{j} $$

By the commutativity of the following diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\times\mathrm{inv}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{mult}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{1}} $$

we learn that

$$ \bigoplus_{k}\mathscr{F}^{i}_{k}\otimes\mathrm{inv}^{*}(\mathscr{F}^{k}_{j})\simeq(\mathscr{O}_{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}})^{\delta_{ij}}. $$

Because $\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is indecomposable as an object of $\QCoh({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ , setting $j=i$ in Equation 29 we learn that for each $i$ there is a unique $k$ such that

$$ \mathscr{F}^{i}_{k}\otimes\mathrm{inv}^{*}(\mathscr{F}^{k}_{i})\simeq\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}} $$

and for all other values of $k$ , the sheaf $\mathscr{F}^{i}_{k}$ is zero. Note in particular that Equation 30 implies that the sheaf $\mathscr{F}^{i}_{k}$ is invertible. Setting $j=k$ in Equation 29, we see that

$$ \mathscr{F}^{i}_{k}\otimes\mathrm{inv}^{*}(\mathscr{F}^{k}_{k})\oplus\mathscr{G}\simeq(\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}})^{\delta_{ik}} $$

for some sheaf $\mathscr{G}$ . Since $i_{1}^{*}(\mathscr{F}^{k}_{k})\neq 0$ , it follows that the left hand side of Equation 31 is nonzero, which implies that $k=i$ . All in all, we have shown that

$$ \mathscr{F}^{i}_{j}=\begin{cases}\mathscr{L}_{i}&i=j\\
0&i\neq j\end{cases} $$

where $\mathscr{L}_{i}$ is some invertible sheaf in $\QCoh({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ . In fact, the coaction of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ on $\mathscr{C}$ endows each $\mathscr{L}_{i}$ with the structure of a multiplicative line bundle over ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . A trivialization of the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ on $\mathscr{C}$ amounts to a trivialization of each $\mathscr{L}_{i}$ as a multiplicative line bundle, so the result follows from the well-known fact that every multiplicative line bundle on ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is (noncanonically) trivializable. ∎

#### Proposition 6.3.0.

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a split semisimple dg category with an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . If $\mathrm{act}_{0}$ is conservative, then the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is trivializable.

#### Proof.

By Proposition 6.3.0, we know that the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}\subseteq\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is trivializable. It follows that

$$ \mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\simeq\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})^{I}. $$

Moreover, using the trivialization of the ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ action on $\mathscr{C}$ , for every $i\in I$ we can endow $k_{i}=\mathrm{ins}_{i}(k)$ with a ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -equivariant structure. Let $n_{i}$ denote the infimum of the $n$ such that $k_{i}\in\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq n}$ . If $n_{i}=-\infty$ , then $\mathrm{act}_{0}(k_{i})=0$ . Otherwise, by changing the trivialization of the ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ action we may set $n_{i}=0$ . ∎

#### 6.3.1.

For completeness, let’s give an example of a split semisimple category with an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ such that $\mathrm{act}_{0}$ isn’t conservative. We will take the category $\mathscr{C}$ to be $\Vect$ ; it remains to specify the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action. Note that the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\times{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{A}^{1}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{G}_{m}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{A}^{1}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{mult}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j\times j} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{mult}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j} $$

is Cartesian (here $j:{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is the canonical embedding). It follows that the functor $j^{*}:\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1})\to\QCoh({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ is symmetric monoidal (where the source and target have the convolution symmetric monoidal structures), and our strange $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on $\Vect$ is given by restricting the trivial ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -action along $j^{*}$ . Since $j^{*}(\delta_{0})=0$ , this action evidently has the property that $\mathrm{act}_{0}=0$ .

### 6.4. A renormalization of $\mathscr{B}_{c}$

#### 6.4.1.

The goal of this section is to prove that $HH(\mathscr{B}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{J}_{c};\id)$ . To do this, we first need to introduce an auxiliary category, which we will call $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathrm{ren}}$ .

Let $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{dual}}$ denote the small subcategory of $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ consisting of objects which are both left- and right-dualizable.

#### Proposition 6.4.1.

An object $x\in\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ lies in $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{dual}}$ if and only if $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}(x)$ is compact in $\mathscr{J}_{c}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}$ is monoidal, if $x$ is both left- and right-dualizable then $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}(x)$ has this property as well, which implies that $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}(x)$ is compact in $\mathscr{J}_{c}\otimes\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ by Proposition 5.3.2. Conversly, suppose that $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}(x)$ is compact. It follows that $\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}(x)$ is concentrated in finitely many degrees, and we claim that this implies that $\tau_{\leq n}x=0$ for $n\ll 0$ . Indeed, for $n\ll 0$ , the object $\tau_{\leq n}x$ lies in the intersection

$$ \bigcap_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\mathscr{B}_{c,\leq n}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}. $$

The composite functor

$$ \mathscr{B}_{c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}\to\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H} $$

is conservative and left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, so it follows that $\tau_{\leq n}x=0$ for $n$ sufficiently negative. Now it follows that $x$ can be written as a finite colimit of its graded pieces, each of which is dualizable, so $x$ itself must be dualizable. ∎

#### 6.4.2.

Now let $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{ren}}$ denote $\Ind(\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{dual}})$ . Because $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is semi-rigid, every compact object fo $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ lies in $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{dual}}$ . It follows that we obtain a pair of adjoint functors

$$ \mathrm{ren}:\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{ren}}:\textrm{un-ren} $$

which exhibit $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ as a colocalization of $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{ren}}$ . Because $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{dual}}$ is a small monoidal subcategory of $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , the category $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{ren}}$ acquires a monoidal structure such that un-ren is monoidal. With respect to this monoidal structure, $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{ren}}$ is tautologically rigid.

Because $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{dual}}$ is stable under the action of $\Perf(B{\mathbf{G}_{m}})\subseteq\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ , the category $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{ren}}$ acquires a $\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ -module structure such that un-ren is $\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ -linear. Let’s write $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathrm{ren}}$ for the de-equivariantization of $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}},\mathrm{ren}}$ . Finally, if we define
